analysis.one_liner: Requires hospitals, nursing homes, and social service employers to run workplace violence prevention plans to protect their workers.
analysis.headline: The bill went to the Senate health committee in March 2019 with 31 cosponsors, all Democrats and one Independent, and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Health care and social service workers face some of the highest rates of physical assault on the job, largely from patients and clients. This bill would order the Labor Department to write a binding federal safety standard requiring covered employers—hospitals, nursing homes, psychiatric facilities, home health agencies, emergency responders, and similar settings—to create written violence prevention plans, assess risks with front-line workers, investigate incidents, train staff annually, keep incident logs, and report violence data to the government each year. It also bans employers from retaliating against workers who report threats or attacks, and ties Medicare funding for some hospitals and nursing homes to compliance.
analysis.who_benefits: Health care and social service workers—nurses, aides, home health visitors, emergency responders, and social service staff—who are exposed to violence from patients, clients, and visitors. They would gain enforceable prevention plans, annual training, faster hazard corrections, incident investigations, and protection from retaliation for reporting.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Health care and social service workers

how_it_helps.text: Employers in covered settings must develop a written workplace violence prevention plan with the participation of direct-care employees and tailor it to each facility's actual hazards [S3].

Employers must investigate violent incidents, provide annual in-person training, keep detailed violent incident logs, post annual summaries, and report violence data to the Labor Department each year [S3].

The bill prohibits employers from retaliating against workers for reporting workplace violence to the employer, law enforcement, or a government agency, and allows the requirement to be enforced like any OSHA standard [S3].
Hospitals and skilled nursing facilities that are not otherwise covered by OSHA rules would have to comply with the standard as a condition of participating in Medicare [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Covered employers—hospitals, nursing homes, home health agencies, behavioral health and social service providers, and staffing firms—bear the cost of security improvements, staffing adjustments, training, investigations, and recordkeeping. In some cases those costs may be passed to patients or payers, and Medicare participation becomes conditional for some facilities.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health care and social service employers

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall on covered employers—engineering controls, security staff, training, and recordkeeping—straining budgets at nursing homes, community clinics, and small social service providers [S3].

A good-faith objection: violence in these settings often stems from patients' medical conditions or community under-resourcing rather than employer negligence, so mandating prevention plans may not reduce attacks as much as supporters hope while still adding significant administrative burden [S3].

The bill directs the Labor Department to issue an interim standard within one year while bypassing the normal OSHA rulemaking process, allowing only a 30-day public comment period, which narrows employer and provider input before rules take effect [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: an enforceable, uniform safety standard in sectors where workers are routinely assaulted, with the strongest protection—annual training, incident logging, and anti-retaliation rights—going to low-wage direct-care staff. The main cost is compliance expense for employers, some of it substantial for security staffing and controls, and the fast-track rulemaking gives affected employers limited input. On balance the bill's protections for workers outweigh the compliance burden, though the burden is not trivial for small providers.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate referred the bill to its Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Tammy Baldwin introduced the bill on March 14, 2019, joined by 31 cosponsors (30 Democrats and 1 Independent) [S4].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day [S5].
That referral was the bill's last action; no markup, floor vote, or House action followed before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health care and social service employers came out ahead: because the bill died in committee, they face no federal workplace violence prevention mandate, no incident-logging and reporting requirements, and no new training or security costs.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health care and social service employers

for.name: Sen. Tammy Baldwin
for.role: Lead sponsor, U.S. Senator from Wisconsin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Workplace Violence Prevention for Health Care and Social Service Workers Act and recruited 31 cosponsors.

for.name: 31 Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republicans signed on.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.role: Committee of referral under Chairman Lamar Alexander (R-TN)
against.what_they_did: Never took up the bill; it received no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action in the 116th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 31 cosponsors were Democrats plus one Independent; no Senate Republican sponsored or cosponsored the bill, and the Republican-chaired HELP Committee never scheduled it for consideration [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would have required written violence prevention plans, engineering controls, annual training, incident logs, and yearly reporting to Labor, with Medicare participation conditioned on compliance for some facilities [S3].

industries.industry: Nursing homes, long-term care, and residential treatment facilities
industries.note: Explicitly covered facilities; they would have faced the full plan, training, logging, and reporting requirements, and non-OSHA-covered facilities would have had to comply to stay in Medicare [S3].

industries.industry: Home health and behavioral/social service providers, and staffing firms
industries.note: Home-based care, emergency transport, correctional-facility clinics, and group homes are covered services, and contractors, temp agencies, and employee-leasing firms are covered employers—so compliance costs would reach small and community providers [S3].
